422-the-romany-rye:
George Borrow continues his wandering tale in this sequel to Lavengro, opening in a damp dingle at dawn. The narrator, camped with gypsies, mends a chaise wheel, tends his forge, and talks with Belle, Isopel Berners, and other road folk. Gypsy lore, horse deals, and sharp talk fill the roadside days.

Borrow mixes travel, language study, and picaresque jest, with long talks on books, faith, and fair play. The Romany Rye of the title names both the road and its free spirit. The book charms as a rambling portrait of England seen from the campfire, not the coach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herve-auguste:
Hervé-Auguste-Étienne-Albans Faye was a French astronomer, born at Saint-Benoît-du-Sault in October 1814 and dead at Paris in 1902. Son of a civil engineer, he entered the École Polytechnique in 1832, left early, and joined the Paris Observatory as a pupil in 1836. There he discovered the periodic comet that bears his name in 1843, winning the Prix Lalande, and he entered the Academy of Sciences in 1847.

Faye taught geodesy at the École Polytechnique, served as rector at Nancy, and held the astronomy chair at the École Polytechnique from 1873 to 1893. He also led the Bureau des Longitudes and served briefly as minister of public instruction in 1877. His fame rests on practical and theoretical work alike, from better methods of measurement and a zenithal collimator to early uses of photography in astronomy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-de-la-ha:
Jean de La Haye, a French Franciscan Bible scholar born in Paris in 1593 and dead there in 1661. He spent his boyhood in Spain and took the habit in the Alcantarine reform. He lectured in philosophy and divinity, preached with distinction, and from 1620 held high offices in his order and at Louis XIII's court.

De La Haye authored or edited some forty folio volumes. He edited Bernardine of Siena, Francis, and Anthony of Padua, and wrote preaching commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, and Revelation. His monuments are the Biblia Magna of 1643 and the nineteen-volume Biblia Maxima of 1660, both built on the Vulgate with gathered commentaries and variant readings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sieur-de-lave: La Vérendrye was the explorer of the Canadian west. This entry traces his forts, his sons, and his fame. The pathfinder of the prairies: his wooden forts dotted the west in the 1730s' decades in the prairies of the north.
doe-osti-3010923-integration-and-validat: Cyber armor in layers got its DOE drill, and this text tests every stacked defense. The pages detail the RD2C results. The security folks get their method. The armor was multi-layer. The drill was DOE's. The defenses were stacked.
narrative-of-a-mission-to-central-africa:
James Richardson led a British mission into Central Africa in 1850 and 1851. Her Majesty's Government ordered and paid for the trip. Richardson had written Travels in the Great Desert of Sahara. Chapman and Hall issued this account in London in 1853.

Richardson died on the journey and left a vast journal behind. His editor shaped eight small, close-written volumes into two books. Dispatches and loose memos filled out the record. The mission crossed the Sahara toward the great lakes and Sudan. Its reports opened Central Africa to British trade and science, at the cost of its leader's life.
nasa-tm-19680026299-cylindrical-electros:
J. A. Findlay and L. H. Brace of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this July 1968 preprint, X-623-68-281, on cylindrical electrostatic probes flown on two satellites. Alouette II and Explorer 31 carried identical probe sensors into the ionosphere. Flying the same instrument on both craft gave scientists a common yardstick for comparing direct measurements between missions.

The report explains the probe theory, the sensors and electronics, and how electron temperature and density are read. Satellite differences still changed data formats and experiment voltages, the authors note. On Alouette II, the topside sounder interfered strongly with probe data. Processing that data proved difficult, they add, though not impossible.
podcast-dannyjones-ABAvPuhu9yE:
Historian Richard Dolan built his reputation on books about UFO secrecy and a possible breakaway civilization. With Danny Jones, he turns from the sky to the sea. He presents what he calls the best evidence that unknown intelligences live deep under the oceans. It is a realm he dubs an underwater Area 51.

Dolan reviews sightings of objects entering and leaving the water at impossible speeds, many from military witnesses. The ocean is the least observed part of the planet, and his argument leans on that darkness. The claims are Dolan's, offered in his measured style, and they remain unproven. Listeners who follow his work get his full underwater case in one sitting, argued by the field's best-known historian rather than its loudest voices.
podcast-joerogan-3eZnbWTb1YE:
Dakota Meyer, a Marine veteran and Medal of Honor recipient, tells Rogan about turning to ibogaine therapy for PTSD. In a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience, Meyer speaks as a man who tried standard care first and kept looking when it fell short.

He describes the treatment itself, a strong psychedelic given in a clinic setting, and the shift he felt afterward. Rogan asks what the nightmares and anger were like before, and what changed after. The segment adds a first-hand voice to the wider debate over psychedelic care for veterans who carry war home with them.
the-romany-rye:
Transcribed from the 1907 J. M. Dent edition, The Romany Rye opens with a chapter headed by the making of a linch-pin, a sound sleeper, breakfast, and a postillion's departure. No author's name is printed in the pages shown.

The narrator wakes at daybreak in a dingle, lights his forge, and fashions a replacement linch-pin for a chaise wheel, copying the pin from the companion wheel. Belle watches near the forge while the postillion sleeps so soundly in the tent that the narrator jokes he must descend from one of the seven sleepers. Fitted and polished, the new pin lets them put the wheel back on.
travels-in-the-united-states-of-america-:
William Priest, a theatre musician from Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Boston, published his American travels at London in 1802. The title page dates his stay from 1793 to 1797. His journals of two Atlantic crossings form part of the book.

Priest's preface admits he wrote the account for friends after coming home in 1797. Only their urging, pressed for three months, brought it to print. He credits extracts from Jefferson, Belknap, and other American writers for much of its value. Readers get a working musician's plain view of the young United States, offered without claims to fine writing.
